In 1869 planters in Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, found a fungus on their coffee leaves. This coffee rust spread over the next twenty years and wiped out what had been one of the world's great coffee industries.

The fungus forms orange powdery spots on the leaves. Infected bushes drop their leaves and give few beans. Ceylon's estates were huge stands of a single crop, so the spores spread easily on the wind. Harvests and exports fell steeply through the 1870s and 1880s.

The government sent the young botanist Harry Marshall Ward to study it in 1880. He warned of the risk of growing one crop everywhere. That was an early lesson in plant pathology, as was the potato blight behind Ireland's Great Famine.

Planters turned to cinchona, the source of quinine, and above all to tea. Within a generation Ceylon tea had replaced coffee. The rust went on to reach the coffee regions of India and Java, and in 1970 Brazil, the largest grower of all. It is still the most damaging disease of coffee.
